Consider a process executing on an operating system that uses demand paging. The average time for a memory access in the system is M units if the corresponding memory page is available in memory, and D units if the memory access causes a page fault. It has been experimentally measured that the average time taken for a memory access in the process is X units.
Which one of the following is the correct expression for the page fault rate experienced by the process?

With page fault rate p: [latex]X=(1-p)M+pD=M+p(D-M)[/latex].

[latex]p=\frac{X-M}{D-M}[/latex]

Answer: (X - M) / (D - M)

questions.question:
Processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4 [/latex] arrive in that order at times 0, 1, 2, and 8 milliseconds respectively, and have execution times of 10, 13, 6, and 9 milliseconds respectively. Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) algorithm is used as the CPU scheduling policy. Ignore context switching times.
Which ONE of the following correctly gives the average turnaround time of the four processes in milliseconds?
questions.explanation:
Simulate SRTF (always run whichever available process has the least remaining time):

[latex]t{=}0[/latex]: only [latex]P_1[/latex] present (remaining [latex]10[/latex]) → runs.
[latex]t{=}1[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]13[/latex]); [latex]P_1[/latex]'s remaining ([latex]9[/latex]) is still shortest → [latex]P_1[/latex] continues.
[latex]t{=}2[/latex]: [latex]P_3[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]6[/latex]); now shortest among [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_3[/latex]([latex]6[/latex]) is [latex]P_3[/latex] → switch to [latex]P_3[/latex].
[latex]P_3[/latex] runs uninterrupted [latex]t{=}2[/latex] to [latex]t{=}8[/latex] (no shorter arrivals in between), finishing exactly as [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives. [latex]P_3[/latex] turnaround [latex]=8-2=6[/latex].
[latex]t{=}8[/latex]: [latex]P_4[/latex] arrives (remaining [latex]9[/latex]); comparing [latex]P_1[/latex]([latex]8[/latex]), [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]), [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_1[/latex] shortest, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}16[/latex]. [latex]P_1[/latex] turnaround [latex]=16-0=16[/latex].
[latex]t{=}16[/latex]: [latex]P_2[/latex]([latex]13[/latex]) vs [latex]P_4[/latex]([latex]9[/latex]) → [latex]P_4[/latex] runs to completion at [latex]t{=}25[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=25-8=17[/latex].
[latex]t{=}25[/latex]: only [latex]P_2[/latex] left, runs to completion at [latex]t{=}38[/latex]. Turnaround [latex]=38-1=37[/latex].

Average turnaround [latex]=\dfrac{6+16+17+37}4=\dfrac{76}4=19[/latex]

Answer: 19

questions.question: With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks
options.B: Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed
options.C: An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource
options.D: A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock

questions.explanation:
Evaluating each deadlock-related statement:

- "Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks" — FALSE. Banker's algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (it checks resource requests dynamically to keep the system in a safe state); deadlock prevention refers to a different set of techniques that structurally rule out one of the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait).
- "Deadlock formation can be prevented by disallowing hold-and-wait" — true: this is a standard, valid deadlock-prevention technique (one of the four necessary conditions is removed).
- "An assignment edge in a resource-allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource" — FALSE. It's the reverse: an assignment edge goes from a resource to a process (resource is allocated to the process); a request edge goes from a process to a resource.
- "A safe state guarantees all processes can finish without deadlock" — true: this is precisely the definition of a safe state.

Answer (the FALSE statements): "Banker's algorithm prevents deadlocks", and "an assignment edge goes from process to resource."

questions.question:
A computer system supports a logical address space of [latex]2^{32}[/latex] bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into a [latex]b[/latex]-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of [latex]b[/latex] is ___________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Page size [latex]=4096=2^{12}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset needs [latex]12[/latex] bits. Logical address space [latex]=2^{32}[/latex] bytes, so the remaining [latex]32-12=20[/latex] bits form the combined page-number field, split between the outer index ([latex]b[/latex] bits) and the inner-page-table offset.

Since each inner page table must itself fit exactly within one page (standard assumption for multi-level paging), and each entry is [latex]8[/latex] bytes, the inner page table holds [latex]\dfrac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries — so the inner-table offset field needs [latex]9[/latex] bits.

[latex]b=20-9=11[/latex]

Answer: 11

In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:
The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.
A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:

1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.

With the OS able to correctly predict only the next [latex]4[/latex] references (including the current one) at the moment a frame is allocated, simulate the reference string [latex]1,3,2,4,2,3,1,2,4,3,1,4[/latex] with [latex]3[/latex] initially-empty frames:

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Ref}&\text{Frames after}&\text{Fault?}\\\hline1&\{1\}&\text{Fault}\\3&\{1,3\}&\text{Fault}\\2&\{1,3,2\}&\text{Fault}\\4&\{4,3,2\}\ (\text{evict }1\text{, unused within next window }2,3,1)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\1&\{4,2,1\}\ (\text{evict }3\text{, farthest-future within window }2,4,3)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,1,3\}\ (\text{evict }2\text{, no longer used in remaining string})&\text{Fault}\\1&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\end{array}[/latex]

Total page faults [latex]=6[/latex] (at references [latex]1,3,2,4,1,3[/latex] in the sequence, marked "Fault" above).

questions.question: Consider four processes P, Q, R, and S scheduled on a CPU as per round robin algorithm with a time quantum of 4 units. The processes arrive in the order P, Q, R, S, all at time t = 0. There is exactly one context switch from S to Q, exactly one context switch from R to Q, and exactly two context switches from Q to R. There is no context switch from S to P. Switching to a ready process after the termination of another process is also considered a context switch. Which one of the following is NOT possible as CPU burst time (in time units) of these processes?
questions.explanation:
Simulate round robin (quantum 4, order P, Q, R, S) for option 4: P = 3, Q = 7, R = 7, S = 3.
- P runs 3 and finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q runs 4 (3 left) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R runs 4 (3 left) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S runs 3 and finishes
- [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q runs 3 and finishes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R runs 3 and finishes

Switches: P[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R, R[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]S, S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R. There is no R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q switch, but exactly one is required. So these burst times are impossible.

(Simulating the other three options gives exactly one S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, one R[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Q, two Q[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]R and no S[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]P.)

Answer: P = 3, Q = 7, R = 7, S = 3

questions.question: Consider a paging system that uses 1-level page table residing in main memory and a TLB for address translation. Each main memory access takes 100 ns and TLB lookup takes 20 ns. Each page transfer to/from the disk takes 5000 ns. Assume that the TLB hit ratio is 95%, page fault rate is 10%. Assume that for 20% of the total page faults, a dirty page has to be written back to disk before the required page is read from disk. TLB update time is negligible. The average memory access time in ns (round off to 1 decimal places) is ___________
questions.explanation:
TLB lookup (20 ns) always happens.
- TLB hit (0.95): 1 memory access = 100 ns
- TLB miss (0.05): page table access 100 ns, then
[latex]\quad[/latex]no fault (0.9): 100 ns
[latex]\quad[/latex]fault (0.1): read page 5000 ns + dirty write-back (20%) 0.2 [latex]\times[/latex] 5000 + access 100 = 6100 ns

[latex]20+0.95(100)+0.05\,[100+0.9(100)+0.1(6100)]=20+95+0.05(800)=155[/latex] ns

Answer: 155

questions.question:
Consider the procedure below for the Producer-Consumer problem which uses semaphores:

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: The producer will be able to add an item to the buffer, but the consumer can never consume it.
options.B: The consumer will remove no more than one item from the buffer.
options.C: Deadlock occurs if the consumer succeeds in acquiring semaphore s when the buffer is empty
options.D: The starting value for the semaphore n must be 1 and not 0 for deadlock-free operation.

questions.explanation:
The consumer does semWait(s) before semWait(n).

If the buffer is empty (n = 0) and the consumer gets s first, it blocks on n while holding s. The producer then blocks on semWait(s) and can never signal n [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] deadlock.

Answer: Deadlock occurs if the consumer succeeds in acquiring semaphore s when the buffer is empty
